summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, enacted in 2014, has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; CBS News and the Associated Press reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned in the province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later Aceh enforcement incident is documented in this record.

Trans people in Aceh have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in Aceh in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.
tangentialFactors:
The UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, but its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific, and it supplies no Aceh figure or measurement period; it also covers the January 2018 detention of twelve trans women, the Aceh incident described in the summary.

Aceh legal scholarship engages directly with waria as a law-enforcement question: 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' (QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture, doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405), by scholars at UIN Ar-Raniry, analyses the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens, indicating that local academic discourse frames transgender presence as a matter for policing rather than protection.

Indonesia-wide reporting notes that transgender people have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more popular in Indonesia; Aceh is the province where that tendency is written into enforceable criminal law.
localsOnly:
The Qanun's special-autonomy authority was granted for Muslim residents, so the sharia criminal layer is framed as applying to the Muslim population of the province; the sources do not state how the provision is applied to non-Muslim residents.

The Ministry of Home Affairs outreach running since June 2021 to issue identification papers, including Kartu Tanda Penduduk, to transgender Indonesians covers Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. Aceh is not among the listed provinces. The programme recognises only male and female descriptors, with no third gender or X option, and prints gender at birth unless court recognition has already been obtained.

Transgender Indonesians may change legal gender on official documents after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which they may marry a person of the opposite legal gender. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it difficult to maintain legitimate employment.

Beauty salons run by transgender people have been a specific target of enforcement in Aceh: the January 2018 North Aceh action closed salons alongside the arrests.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 is applied to non-Muslim visitors, or to conduct occurring outside the province, is not resolved in the sources; only the 2005 grant of authority framed in terms of Muslim residents is documented.

No Aceh-specific figure for violence against trans people, with a denominator and a general homicide rate for comparison, is available in this record, so no trans-specific rate for the province can be stated.

The record contains no Aceh enforcement incident dated after 26 August 2025. Whether caning or arrest has continued since that date is not sourced here, and the absence of a later documented case is not evidence that enforcement has stopped.

Entry, visa and airport-screening treatment specific to Aceh, and any Aceh-specific document-marker flagging beyond the national ID outreach noted above, are not sourced in this inventory.
